problem.title: Every new session starts by searching
problem.body: A new session does not know your layout, so it lists folders, greps and opens files to find its way. Stacklit gives it a map first. In our test the same questions took {grepControl} Grep and Glob calls without the map and {grepArm} with it. The agent can still grep when it needs to.

citation.text: In one study of eight models on SWE-bench Verified, the higher cost runs repeated file views and edits more, and three of the higher cost models repeated around half of their file actions on the same file.
citation.source: Bai et al., How Do AI Agents Spend Your Money? (arXiv 2604.22750)
citation.caveat: This describes the waste in other agents. It is not our result. One preprint, one benchmark.

items.name: Map it
items.text: One command scans the repo with tree-sitter and writes stacklit.json, a dependency diagram and a visual map, then opens the map in your browser.

items.name: Wire it up
items.text: Setup finds the assistants on your machine and writes the config each one reads. It also installs git hooks that rebuild the map after commits, checkouts and merges.

items.name: Ask where
items.text: Your agent asks a plain question and gets a ranked file list that fits a token budget. Slice prints one symbol's source. Impact lists what depends on it.

proof.title: How well does it find the right file?
proof.intro: We asked 47 where-is-it questions over six public repos and checked which file a simple script would open first. No AI model was involved. With one short query, Stacklit put the right file first on 81% of them and in the top five on 96%.
proof.note: Grep with a pattern written by someone who knew the answer did better: 89% first, 100% in the top five. Plain keyword search did worse at the first file, 57%. We tuned Stacklit on these questions, so treat 81% as a best case. On 40 fresh questions from our own repo the right file came first on 28 and in the top five on all 40. No AI model was involved here. The agent results above come from real sessions.
proof.sizes: For scale, the whole map of a repo is {range} tokens. A token is a small chunk of text, about three quarters of a word.

items: Free and MIT. There is no paid tier.
One Go binary that runs on your machine.
No AI model builds the map. The same repo always gives the same map.
One optional command, init --summary, sends module names (never file contents) to a command you choose. It is off by default.
Every number links to its method in the repo, including the ones that make us look worse.

items.q: Will it lower my token bill?
items.a: No, not overall. We ran two tests ({allSessions} sessions in all). On the biggest repo (about 16,000 files) a session cost {levelrailDropLow}% to {levelrailDropHigh}% less. On repos of a few thousand files or fewer it cost more: {r2SmallRiseMin}% to {r2SmallRiseMax}% more in the second test, and {featuredropRise}% more on the 400 file repo in the first. Averaged over all four repos, a session cost {r2PooledRiseE}% to {r2PooledRiseA}% more, depending on the wording, not less. What fell was the work: {grepFewerLow}% to {grepFewerHigh}% fewer grep and glob searches, a quarter to a third fewer tool calls, about a fifth fewer turns. Questions like "who imports X" cost about {impactRatio} times as much in the first test. So today it is for very large repos and "where is it" questions, and not yet for small repos. Dollar figures are Claude Code's own estimates at list prices, for one model and questions we wrote. The full tables are on the agent test page.

No. In the first test answers were slightly less often right with Stacklit: {correctControl}% without it, {correctArm}% with it, on the grader we fixed in advance. After we corrected three grading mistakes of ours it was {auditedControl}% against {auditedArm}%, and that gap could be chance. The losses were mostly on questions that need several files, where the agent stopped after one query. In the second test answers were equally often right: {r2CorrectControl}% without it, {r2CorrectA}% with it. The detail is on the agent test page.

Often grep is enough, and for an exact name it is better: on 'who imports X' questions it was cheaper. Stacklit helps when the question is a plain sentence with no name to grep, and on big repos. In our two tests agents with the map ran {grepFewerLow}% to {grepFewerHigh}% fewer Grep and Glob calls and a quarter to a third fewer tool calls overall. The map is also one file in git that every assistant reads and a pull request can review.

items.q: Does 82% fewer searches mean 82% less work?
items.a: No. The agent swapped most greps for Stacklit queries. Tool calls fell by a quarter to a third and turns by about a fifth. Cost did not follow: it fell on the biggest repo and rose on smaller ones.

items.q: Does it keep the map fresh?
items.a: A git hook rebuilds it after commits, checkouts and merges. In Claude Code an optional hook refreshes it after each edit, and stacklit watch keeps the symbol graph current. Edits made by hand while none of these run wait for the next run. Use stacklit refresh or stacklit generate.

items.q: Does it send my code anywhere?
items.a: No. It runs locally with no account and no telemetry. The one exception is the optional init --summary, which pipes module names and exports, no file contents, to a command you configure. This website makes no third party requests. The generated map pages request small language logos from thesvg.org unless you turn that off with STACKLIT_MAP_ICONS=off.

final.title: Give your agent a map
final.text: One command, free, MIT. Commit the map and every assistant on your team starts from the same page.

meta.title: Stacklit: stop making your AI re-read your codebase
meta.description: Stacklit maps your repo once. In 1,100 test sessions, agents ran 78% to 82% fewer grep and glob searches. Cheaper on a huge repo, dearer on small ones. Free, MIT, Go.
meta.structured: Stacklit is a free, MIT licensed command line tool that writes a small committed map of a codebase for AI coding agents, with token budgeted queries for files, symbols and dependents.
meta.llms: Stacklit writes a small map of your codebase into git so coding agents start from the layout. A 19,500 line Go repo (gin v1.10.0) becomes a 137 token map (tokens are bytes divided by 4). It parses a repository with tree-sitter and writes stacklit.json, a dependency diagram and an interactive HTML map, and sets up 25 assistants including Claude Code, Cursor and Codex. The map is built without an LLM or embeddings. Free, MIT, one Go binary, no account, no telemetry. In our benchmark a 1,000 token query puts the right file first on 81% of questions, and grep with a hand written pattern does better at 89%; it is a benchmark, not an agent study. In two separate tests of real Claude Code sessions (450, then 650) on four public repos, Stacklit cut tool calls by a quarter to a third but did not lower cost: cheaper on the largest repo (about 16,000 files, 11% to 22% less), more expensive on the smaller ones, and about 9% to 17% more on average across the four repos in the second test.

agentTest.title: What happened in real agent sessions
agentTest.intro: We ran Claude Code on public repos, with and without Stacklit, in two tests: {sessions} sessions, then {r2Sessions} more, each with the plan written down before the first run. Stacklit changed how the agent works. It was cheaper on the biggest repo, more expensive on smaller ones, and not cheaper overall.
agentTest.tableCaption: Cost of a session with Stacklit divided by the same session without it, with a 95% interval. Below 1 means cheaper. 50 paired sessions per repo, {pairs} in all. Cost is the CLI's notional list price.
helps: Big repos. On the largest one (about 16,000 files) a session cost {levelrailDropLow}% to {levelrailDropHigh}% less, in both tests.
Questions like "where is X?" when you do not know the name.
Questions like "where should a new thing go?"
fails: Small repos. On repos of 400 to 3,000 files a session cost more, up to {r2SmallRiseMax}% more. Averaged over all four repos it cost more, not less.
Following a path across several files. In the first test answers were right {traceArm}% of the time with Stacklit, against {traceControl}% without.
Exact names. If you already know the name, plain grep is better. Questions like "who imports X" cost about {impactRatio} times as much with Stacklit.
The strict setup (it blocks the agent from crawling) was worse. It is off by default.
agentTest.limits: Limits: one model (Sonnet), 70 questions we wrote, four repos, two days. Most questions needed only one or two exact greps. The model had partly memorised one repo (featuredrop), which favours the side without Stacklit. Editing tasks, other models and harder reasoning were not tested.
